name: Flatline Kids — Pre-Digital Revivalist Youth
description: The Flatline Kids are a youth movement obsessed with the pre-internet analog era of the late 20th century — not the pop nostalgia of the Nineties Church, but the deeper, quieter texture of life before connectivity: rotary phones, physical mail, cash transactions, and the specific loneliness of being unreachable. Concentrated in Tier 1-2 populations who never had reliable BCI access anyway, Flatline Kids reframe their infrastructural exclusion as a spiritual aesthetic, collecting pre-2000 artifacts from ghost markets and ghost-running 'dead drop' social networks using physical handwritten notes left at coded locations across GLMZ. Their fashion centers on deliberate blandness — muted earth tones, unbranded fabric, no visible chrome — as a radical refusal of the signal economy. Internal disputes center on 'authenticity depth': purists who reject all post-1980 technology versus 'surface flats' who engage selectively. The movement's zine, *No Carrier*, is hand-printed on reclaimed paper and distributed only through dead-drop networks.
cultural_impact: Flatline Kids have revived a small-scale physical mail and dead-drop communication infrastructure across the Gray Zone districts that has been quietly adopted by criminal networks and political dissidents who value its near-total invisibility to corporate surveillance systems. Their aesthetic has also influenced a minor Tier 3 fashion trend for 'signal-blank' clothing.
locations: The Pale Room — a Tier 1 basement zine library, District 4 the Gray Zone
Corrigan's Hardware — a front-business dead-drop hub, Tier 2 North Side
story_hooks: A Flatline Kids dead-drop note contains coordinates and a partial map that appears to lead to a pre-corporate infrastructure node — something buried before GLMZ was incorporated — and multiple parties want to know what's there.

The movement's founding figure, known only as 'Carrier,' has disappeared, and the community is fracturing between those who believe they were taken by corporate surveillance and those who think Carrier simply chose to go fully off-grid.

A Tier 4 nostalgia brand has somehow obtained copies of *No Carrier* zines and is producing high-end facsimiles for wealthy collectors — and the Flatline Kids are debating whether to let it happen, weaponize it, or burn it down.
